Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a server-rendered Spring Boot application for browsing, uploading, serving, and deleting photos. It persists photo data and metadata in Oracle Database and can be run with the database using Docker Compose.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle Database is the application's only identified data store. Spring Data JPA and Hibernate access Oracle through the Oracle JDBC driver; photo metadata and image bytes are stored together, with image bytes held as BLOB data. Docker Compose provisions the database alongside the application. No cache, message broker, or external API integration was identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Uses Spring MVC with Thymeleaf for server-rendered gallery and detail pages, with a JSON response for uploads.
  • Separates photo operations behind a service interface and Spring Data JPA repository.
  • Stores uploaded images in Oracle rather than on the application filesystem; Spring Security requires HTTP Basic authentication for uploads and deletion.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes five HTTP routes: server-rendered gallery/detail pages, a multipart upload endpoint with a JSON response, and an endpoint that serves photo bytes. Requests are handled synchronously within one application and synchronously persisted to the database; no inter-service API or asynchronous messaging was found.

DTOs & Contracts

  • Photo is the mutable JPA entity and is also added to MVC models for the gallery and detail views. Its persistence structure is documented separately in data-architecture.md.
  • UploadResult is a mutable service-layer result object used to communicate per-file upload success or failure to the controller; it is not directly serialized as the HTTP response.
  • The upload response is assembled from Java Map instances rather than a dedicated response DTO. Each successful item contains photo metadata, and each failed item contains a filename and error message.
  • No dedicated request DTO is defined; upload input is Spring's MultipartFile binding. The id values are path parameters.
  • No immutable DTOs were found. JSON responses use Spring Boot/Jackson serialization, while gallery and detail responses use Thymeleaf templates.
  • No OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: The browser calls the Spring MVC application over HTTP. Controllers call PhotoService directly; PhotoServiceImpl calls PhotoRepository via Spring Data JPA/JDBC to Oracle. Photo metadata and binary content are stored in the database.
  • Asynchronous: No message broker, event-driven communication, or asynchronous service calls were found.
  • Resilience: No retry, circuit-breaker, timeout, or bulkhead policy was found. Errors are handled locally in some controller/service paths (including upload result errors, redirects, and HTTP 404/500 responses); no downstream-service fallback policy exists.
  • Discovery and gateway: There is no service registry, client-side load balancing, or API gateway. Compose's internal oracle-db hostname is used for database connectivity.
  • Startup dependency: Compose starts the application after the Oracle container reports healthy. This affects whether the application can start and access the database; operational probe and wait details are maintained in configuration-inventory.md.
  • Security: Spring Security configures stateless HTTP Basic authentication for POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete; other routes are permitted anonymously. There is no application-level role check beyond requiring authentication on those state-changing routes. CSRF is disabled. No TLS/HTTPS configuration was found, so transport encryption is not configured in the application.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets users upload, browse, inspect, navigate, and remove photos from a shared gallery. Each accepted photo and its image data are kept together as a persistent gallery item.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto Album / Gallery ManagementA user-contributed image managed as a gallery item, with information used to display and navigate the collection.Each photo is independently addressable in the gallery and is the unit of upload, viewing, navigation, and deletion.
UploadResultPhoto Album / Gallery ManagementThe outcome of processing an individual uploaded file, including its success or failure and any associated photo identifier.Produced for each file submitted to the upload workflow; a successful result identifies the persisted Photo.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

The application is a single deployable Spring MVC application, not a set of independently deployable business services. Its presentation, business operations, and persistence components share the Photo Album bounded context.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
HomeController and DetailControllerGallery presentation and workflowsNone; coordinates gallery operationsPhotoService
PhotoFileControllerPhoto deliveryNone; retrieves image data for displayPhotoService
PhotoServiceImplGallery managementPhoto lifecycle and UploadResult outcomesPhotoRepository; Oracle database through JPA
PhotoRepositoryGallery persistencePersists and queries Photo recordsOracle database

All photo records, including their image data, are owned by this application and stored in Oracle. There are no cross-service APIs, events, or shared cross-context identifiers.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload Photos

An authenticated user submits one or more files through the upload interface to POST /upload. The controller processes each file independently through PhotoService. For each file, the service checks the supported MIME type, configured per-file size limit, non-empty content, and image pixel limit when dimensions can be read. Invalid files receive an individual failure result; accepted data is stored as a Photo in Oracle and returned with its identifier. The controller gathers successful photo summaries and per-file failures, allowing partial success when a batch contains both accepted and rejected files.

Workflow 2: Browse and View a Photo

The gallery page at GET / requests photos ordered newest-first and renders each photo with its metadata. Selecting an item opens GET /detail/{id}; the controller retrieves that photo and asks the service for the adjacent older and newer photos by upload time. The image is served separately from GET /photo/{id} using the Photo's stored image data. If a photo cannot be found, the detail and image handlers return the user to the gallery or return not found, respectively.

Workflow 3: Delete a Photo

An authenticated user submits the delete form to POST /detail/{id}/delete. PhotoService looks up the photo; if present, it deletes that record (including the database-stored image) and the controller reports success. If no photo exists, the controller reports that it was not found. The user is redirected to the gallery.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no cross-service composition or aggregation flows: all business operations run within one application. The PhotoService coordinates with the PhotoRepository, which reads or writes the Photo and its image data in Oracle. Gallery, detail, and image responses are assembled from this same source of truth; no remote-service fallback path is implemented.

Business Workflow Sequence

The upload workflow is the primary business process. Each submitted file is handled independently, so a failed validation or save for one file does not prevent the controller from processing the remaining files.

sequenceDiagram participant User participant Gallery as "Gallery Controller" participant PhotoService as "Photo Service" participant Photo as "Photo" participant Repository as "Photo Repository" participant Oracle as "Oracle Database" User->>Gallery: Submit photo files to POST /upload Gallery->>PhotoService: Process each file PhotoService->>PhotoService: Check file type, size, content, and image dimensions alt File passes upload rules PhotoService->>Photo: Create gallery item with image and metadata PhotoService->>Repository: Save photo Repository->>Oracle: Persist photo record and image data Oracle-->>Repository: Saved photo Repository-->>PhotoService: Photo with identifier PhotoService-->>Gallery: Successful upload result else File fails a rule or cannot be saved PhotoService-->>Gallery: Failed upload result with reason end Gallery-->>User: Report uploaded and failed files

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Supported file types: Upload accepts MIME types configured as JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP.
  • Per-file size and content: Each file must be non-empty and no larger than the configured 10 MiB limit. The HTTP multipart request also has a configured maximum request size.
  • Image dimensions: When image dimensions can be read, images exceeding 40 million pixels are rejected. If dimensions cannot be extracted, upload continues without dimension metadata.
  • Batch outcomes: Each file produces an independent outcome. The response includes successful photo summaries and individual failures; its overall success flag is true when at least one uploaded photo is included.
  • Gallery ordering and navigation: Gallery entries are ordered newest-first. Detail navigation finds older and newer items using upload timestamps.
  • Photo lifecycle: A successful upload creates a persistent Photo; deletion removes it from the gallery and database. No additional business lifecycle states are modeled.
  • Authorization: Gallery and photo reads are public. Upload and delete POST operations require HTTP Basic authentication.
  • Persistence boundary: PhotoService operations use transaction management for database changes. There are no distributed transactions, event-driven side effects, or compensating workflows.
  • Failure handling: Missing photos yield not-found behavior for image retrieval and a not-found message for deletion. Upload validation and persistence failures are represented as per-file errors; no external-service fallback applies.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is the final 2.x release and is outside the community support window; migration to a supported Spring Boot line will also require reviewing Java 8 compatibility, since newer Spring Boot generations require a newer Java baseline. The Oracle JDBC driver is selected through the Boot parent dependency management, so its effective version should be re-evaluated as part of that upgrade.

Notable Observations

  • The parent POM manages versions for all direct dependencies except Commons IO, which is explicitly set to 2.11.0.
  • The Spring Boot Web Starter already provides JSON support; the separately declared JSON starter may duplicate that functionality.
  • The Oracle JDBC driver is runtime-scoped, while H2 is confined to tests.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The application has one JPA entity, Photo, persisted in a relational database through Hibernate. Oracle is configured for the normal and Docker profiles, while tests use an in-memory H2 database.

Entity Model

Photo maps to the photos table and owns its upload metadata and image bytes. The table has an index on uploaded_at. Its identifier is a UUID string generated in Java. There are no entity relationships or join tables. UploadResult is a service response model, not a persisted entity.

Source: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java.

The service implementation applies transaction boundaries at class level, with read-only transactions for retrieval methods: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java. The model's photo_data mapping is nullable even though the normal upload path supplies the photo bytes.

The repository extends JpaRepository<Photo, String>, inheriting standard CRUD operations. The custom queries are native SQL, several of which use Oracle-specific features; no cross-service aggregation methods were found.

Caching Strategy

No application cache provider, cache annotations, cache manager, JCache binding, or Hibernate second-level cache configuration was found. Data access uses repository/database queries without an identified application-level caching pattern or TTL/eviction policy.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The project has one application and one logical data owner. The default and Docker profiles connect to Oracle; the test profile uses an isolated in-memory H2 database. The application reads and writes its own PHOTOS table through Spring Data JPA, with transaction management in the service layer. There are no other services, cross-service database access patterns, or CQRS/read-model boundaries identified.
